L4: # Frequently asked questions
L5: 
L6: Find answers to common questions about ASU’s flexible pathways to college, designed to make higher education accessible and convenient for all learners.
L7: 
L8: 【2†Image: ASU students sitting near palm trees】
L9: ## About
L10: 
L11: What are ASU Universal Learner Courses?
L12: 
L13: Arizona State University offers an expanding list of open-access courses taught by ASU faculty and available for people who are not formally admitted or enrolled at ASU. Universal Learner Courses (or ULCs) often satisfy general studies requirements or are common prerequisites across a variety of majors.
L14: 
L15: Is this the same course I would take on campus?
L16: Yes, Universal Learner Courses provide a course experience that serves diverse learner audiences and features active learning and project-based assessment. These courses are evaluated and designed by ASU faculty to align with the same courses on campus and feature the same faculty.
L17: 
L18: 【3†Image: Paper plane graphic】
L19: ## Registration
L20: 
L21: How do I register?
L22: 
L23: You can register at 【4†ulc.asu.edu】 by clicking on the “Register” button.
L24: 
L25: Do I have to apply to ASU?
L26: 
L27: No, anyone who is not enrolled at ASU can take Universal Learner Courses.
L28: However, if you are planning to pursue a degree at ASU, you must 【5†submit an application†asuonline.asu.edu】 and we highly recommend that you do that as soon as possible so that your transition into ASU upon completion of the program is a seamless experience and we can better support you.
L29: Can current ASU students take these courses?
L30: Admitted, degree-seeking ASU students cannot take ULCs as they are designed for learners who are not yet enrolled at ASU. Included in the tuition are student support services specifically designed to help currently enrolled students persist toward their goal of graduation. If you are an admitted ASU student, please refer to the 【6†ASU Course Catalog†catalog.apps.asu.edu】 for available courses.
L31: An ASU student may become eligible to enroll in ULCs again if they defer their enrollment, or pass the seven term minimum since an active ASU enrollment. The same rules for disqualified ASU students apply to ULC also, so students who are academically disqualified cannot add ULCs to their ASU transcript.
L32: How old do you have to be to take these courses?
L33: 
L34: There are no age restrictions for Universal Learner Courses. However, these are college-level courses and do require identity verification.
L35: 
L36: How do I verify my identity?
L37: ULC learners are required to authenticate their identity before their course begins with a live photo and an approved form of photo identification. This includes government-issued IDs, school IDs, or birth certificates for learners under 18. Your photo ID must match the name associated with your ASU account.
L38: If you’re under the age of 18, you may provide a birth certificate to begin the course, but if your course requires proctoring, a government-issued ID is required to take the exam and complete the course.
L39: Can I get an ASU ID card after I register?
L40: 
L41: No, ASU ID cards are issued to admitted ASU students only.
L42: 
L43: Will I get an asu.edu email after I register for Universal Learner Courses?
L44: 
L45: No, ASU has transitioned away from issuing emails and supports using personal emails. ASU emails are only issued when a course requires it for the completion of the course. Most courses do not require ASU emails for completion. Learners will not retain access to ASU Gmail once they are no longer actively enrolled in ULCs.
L46: 【7†Image: Person in front of whiteboard graphic】
L47: ## Courses
L48: 
L49: When do I need to be online for my courses?
L50: 
L51: Universal Learner Courses are asynchronous which means they do not have any live content. While there are weekly due dates in most courses, you can complete the coursework when it is convenient for you. Some courses hold live office hours with instructors, but these are not required and the content is recorded and posted in the course to view whenever works best for you.
L52: 
L53: Do I need to order any textbooks or materials?
L54: No, you do not need to order any textbooks or materials. All materials are provided when the course opens.
L55: 
L56: How can I get academic support in my courses?
L57: 
L58: Visit the 【8†ULC Online Study Hub†tutoring.asu.edu】 for academic support. You will need to use your ASURITE to access.
L59: 
L60: How do I access my ASU Gmail account?
L61: ASU emails are only issued when a course requires it for the completion of the course. Most courses do not require ASU emails for completion. Sign in to your 【9†My ASU†my.asu.edu】 and select the Gmail shortcut link located in your shortcuts list. If you don’t see the Gmail shortcut link select View More and select Gmail from the drop-down. You can also access your ASU Gmail by going to 【10†email.asu.edu†email.asu.edu】. If you are unable to access your Gmail, please contact 【11†[email protected]】.
L62: If I unenroll, will it appear on my transcript?
L63: 
L64: No. There is no risk to your academic record with Universal Learner Courses since you don’t pay to add them to your transcript until you choose. If you find that now’s not the time for you to take a course, you can easily unenroll at any time on your learner dashboard.
L65: 
L66: What does on-demand and session-based mean?
L67: On-demand is a course you can start today that can be completed at your own pace. You must spend a minimum of 6 weeks enrolled in the course and have 1 year to complete it. Session-based is a course with a specific start date and the structure of a cohort with other learners and due dates.
L68: 
L69: Is on-demand or session-based right for me?
L70: Not all courses are available in both formats but we encourage learners to enroll in session-based courses whenever possible. We find that learners are more successful in session-based courses where they can move through the course material with other learners and have due dates for assignments. On-demand courses are best for learners who have to take long absences from internet connectivity or high school students that use these courses for dual enrollment.
L71: 
L72: How long do I have access to the course?
L73: You’ll have access to the course materials (readings, videos, presentations, etc.) for 2 weeks after the course ends for all session-based courses and on-demand courses will be closed upon request for academic credit.
L74: 
L75: How can I get enrollment verification?
L76: A letter can be written verifying your enrollment in your current Universal Learner Courses. To request a letter, please reach out to our support team at 【12†[email protected]】. This letter can only be sent directly to the learner and cannot be provided to other institutions or organizations.
L77: 
L78: Can I get my student loans deferred while taking Universal Learner Courses?
L79: No, we are unable to complete any loan-related forms. Learners enrolled in Universal Learner Courses are not considered admitted to Arizona State University. At this time, the only documentation we are able to provide is an Enrollment Verification (EV) letter.
L80: 
L81: 【13†Image: Medal graphic】
L82: ## Payment
L83: 
L84: How much are Universal Learner Courses?
L85: 
L86: You’ll pay a $25 course enrollment fee to reserve your place in the course. If you’d like to add the course to your ASU transcript for college credit, you’ll need to pay a fee of $400 following the completion of your course if you are satisfied with your grade.
L87: 
L88: Are there any hidden fees?

L1: # How homeschool students can do dual enrollment online with ASU Universal Learner Courses
L2: 
L3: 【1†Image: A smiling teenage girl wearing a gray turtleneck sits at a wooden desk in a bright room, looking at a laptop while homeschooling.】
L4: 
L5: From middle school exploration to earning college credit in high school, ASU Universal Learner Courses give homeschool students more ways to pursue their interests and prepare for what’s next.
L6: 
L7: 【2†Image†secure.gravatar.com】
L8: 
L9: By Jen Woods
L10: 
L11: November 13, 2026
L12:   * 【3†Learner stories】
L13:   * 【4†Newsroom】
L14:   * 【5†Your questions, answered】
L15: 
L16: For homeschool families, learning can be shaped around a student’s interests, abilities and goals. Some students are ready for advanced subjects earlier than their peers, while others want to experience college-level coursework before deciding what comes after high school.
L17: Through Arizona State University’s Universal Learner Courses (ULCs), homeschool students can take online courses, exploring new subjects and potentially earning college credit before graduating from high school.
L18: 
L19: For Emma Wright, enrolling in an ASU course was an opportunity to see how her academic preparation measured up to university expectations.
L20: “I was working ahead in school. I have homeschooled my whole life. My mom said I was doing well. But I wasn’t sure how I would do in a real class with real teachers,” Wright said. “This program has allowed me to know I can succeed.”
L21: ## How do ASU Universal Learner Courses work as a homeschool dual enrollment program?
L22: 
L23: Universal Learner Courses are online, first and second year college courses designed and taught by ASU faculty. Students pay $25 to enroll and complete the coursework before deciding whether to add the grade to an official ASU transcript.
L24: After receiving their final grade, learners can choose to pay an additional $400 to earn academic credit. If they are not satisfied with their grade, they do not have to add the course to their ASU transcript.
L25: 
L26: Families can choose between session-based courses, which follow established schedules and weekly deadlines, and on-demand courses, which allow students to progress at their own pace. Both formats are asynchronous, making it possible to fit coursework around existing homeschool schedules.
L27: For homeschool families, Universal Learner Courses provide a way to incorporate college level coursework into their high school curriculum without an agreement between a school or district and ASU. Families can determine how completed courses count toward their student’s high school requirements, following applicable state guidelines.
L28: Students can enroll directly in individual courses without applying for admission to ASU, and taking a course does not automatically make them an admitted university student.
L29: > “I was working ahead in school. I have homeschooled my whole life. My mom said I was doing well. But I wasn’t sure how I would do in a real class with real teachers,” Wright said.
L30: > “This program has allowed me to know I can succeed.”
L31: >
L32: > – Emma Wright, homeschool learner
L33: ## Can middle schoolers take college classes?
L34: 
L35: Yes. With no minimum age requirement, Universal Learner Courses give academically prepared middle school students access to college level coursework. For families exploring college courses for middle school students, this can be particularly valuable when a student has advanced beyond their current curriculum or developed a strong interest in a particular subject.
L36: Families should consider whether their student is prepared for independent learning, college-level assignments and managing coursework deadlines. Starting with one course can be a useful way to assess that readiness.
L37: 
L38: Odin Halvorsen enrolled in his first ASU course at 13 years old.
L39: 
L40: “The experience made me feel more independent as a student,” Halvorsen said. “It gave me a preview of what college courses will be like.”
L41: ## How to take college classes in high school
L42: 
L43: For homeschool high school students, Universal Learner Courses can complement an existing curriculum while providing opportunities to explore potential college majors and earn academic credit before graduation.
L44: A student considering a psychology degree, for example, might take an introductory course to better understand the field. Another might choose college mathematics or writing to build on subjects already studied at home. Along the way, students gain experience navigating university coursework, managing assignments and meeting college-level expectations.
L45: 
L46: Audrey Reinhardt has been able to incorporate ASU courses into her homeschool education while managing her own learning schedule.
L47: “I feel more in control of my work and pacing throughout the modules, and it has definitely taught me so much independence that I think will be irreplaceable in the future,” Reinhardt said.
L48: 
L49: She also sees value in the coursework regardless of whether a student chooses to purchase college credit. “Even if you do not end up putting it on your transcript, you still learned valuable information.”
L50: ## Is this homeschool dual enrollment?
L51: 
L52: Homeschool families exploring dual enrollment for homeschoolers can access college-level coursework through ASU Universal Learner Courses, even without an agreement between a high school and a university.
L53: Unlike traditional dual enrollment programs, which typically operate through a school or district, Universal Learner Courses allow families to enroll directly with ASU. Homeschool organizations can also participate through Accelerate ASU, the university’s nationwide dual enrollment program.
L54: ## How to include ASU courses on a homeschool transcript
L55: 
L56: Families can document completed Universal Learner Courses on their homeschool transcript, identifying the coursework as college level study through Arizona State University.
L57: 
L58: If a student chooses to purchase academic credit, the course also appears on an official ASU transcript. Families determine how coursework counts toward high school requirements according to applicable state guidelines, while ASU awards the university credit.
L59: ## Will ASU Universal Learner Courses transfer to other universities?
L60: 
L61: College credit earned through Universal Learner Courses is recorded on an official ASU transcript and may be transferable to other institutions.
L62: Each college or university determines how transferred coursework applies to its degree requirements. Families should check with prospective institutions to understand whether a course will satisfy a general education requirement, count as an elective or apply toward a particular degree program.
L63: ## Frequently asked questions
L64: 
L65: Can homeschoolers do dual enrollment? Yes. Homeschool families can take college-level coursework through 【6†ASU Universal Learner Courses】 without an agreement between a high school and a university. Families enroll directly in ULCs, the same way any other family does.
L66: Is dual enrollment worth it for homeschool students? It can be a low-risk way to try college coursework. Students pay a 【7†$25 enrollment fee】 and complete the course first. If they’re satisfied with their grade, they can pay $400 to 【8†add it to an official ASU transcript】 within one year of finishing.

L115: # Can You Take College Classes in High School? Here’s How
L116: 
L117: Posted on July 17, 2025
L118: 
L119: By Sophia Learning
L120: 
L121: If you’re wondering if you can take college classes in high school, yes, you can! Taking college classes while you’re still in high school is an excellent way to 【103†get ahead in your education】, save money on tuition, and explore college-level coursework.
L122: There are several pathways available for high school students to get a jump on their college education, including Advanced Placement (AP) courses, dual enrollment, summer college classes, and more. Here’s everything you need to know to make a plan.
L123: ## What Is the Earliest You Can Take College Classes?
L124: 
L125: The timeline for taking college classes varies based on the program and institution. Most high school students get a head start on college with AP courses during their high school years, which are developed by the College Board and available in over 30 subjects.
L126: AP courses are often available for students in their junior year, but some other programs allow younger students to take college-level courses. For example, Sophia allows students as young as 13 to take college courses for future credits. Dual enrollment programs also have age- and grade-level requirements that vary by state and institution. The best way to plan is by talking to your school counselor about the opportunities that are available in your area.
L127: ## Summer College Classes for High School Students
L128: 
L129: Many colleges and universities offer 【104†summer programs】 designed specifically for high school students. These classes give you an opportunity to experience college coursework in a more flexible setting and often cover a range of general education subjects, such as college-level math, English, and science.
L130: Some programs are residential, offering an on-campus experience to prepare you for college, while others are available online. Taking summer courses can help lighten your future college course load and provide a glimpse into the rigors of college academics.
L131: ## Online Dual Enrollment Programs for High School Students
L132: 
L133: 【105†Dual enrollment】 programs allow you to take college courses for credit that count toward both your high school diploma requirements and some of the general education credits for your future college degree. Many institutions offer online dual enrollment options, making early college courses more accessible for students with busy schedules and limited transportation options.
L134: Online dual enrollment is a great choice for students looking to earn college credits while managing other responsibilities, like extracurricular activities, without becoming overwhelmed. However, dual enrollment can come with a heavier course load, higher academic expectations, and more demands for studying and assignments.

L140: ## Seek Out Local Colleges That Allow High School Students
L141: 
L142: Seek Out Local Colleges That Allow High School Students
L143: 
L144: Looking into local colleges and universities is another option for taking college classes while in high school. Some community colleges have partnerships with local high schools for both in-person and online courses for eligible students. These colleges may also allow high school students to enroll in specific courses, either for credit or as part of an early college program.
